procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated October 18, 1968 of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 1161 of 1966, allowing the oral application of the respondent's advocate for amendment of the charge and directing a new trial on the amended charge.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The second respondent Bank filed a complaint against the appellant alleging misappropriation. The Magistrate framed a charge under s. 406, Penal Code, for misappropriation of moneys. The appellant was convicted and appealed to the High Court. During the appeal, the High Court allowed an oral application to amend the charge to include misappropriation of goods and directed a new trial on the amended charge, keeping the appeal pending.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the High Court's order, arguing that the order for a new trial was unwarranted, unfair, and unsupported by the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, finding no reason to interfere with the High Court's discretion in framing the charge and giving the accused an opportunity to meet the additional charge.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred by amending the charge and keeping the appeal pending, instead of first delivering a finding on the charge for which the appellant was convicted.

facts: The appellant was convicted by a Magistrate for misappropriation of money under s. 406 of the Penal Code.
The appellant appealed this conviction to the High Court.
During the appeal hearing, the complainant (the Bank) requested to amend the charge to include an alternative charge of misappropriation of goods, which arose from the same transaction.

The High Court allowed the amendment, sent the case back to the Magistrate to give the appellant a full opportunity to defend against the amended charge, and kept the appeal pending until the record of this new proceeding was returned.
law: The Supreme Court noted that the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr. P. C.) grants appellate courts ample power to alter or amend a charge.
Specifically, Section 423 of the Cr. P. C. invests the appellate court with very wide powers, including the power to make any amendment or consequential order that is just or proper.

The primary limitation on this power is that the accused must not be prejudiced, meaning they should not have to face a charge for a new offence or be denied a full opportunity to meet the charge and present a defense.
application: The Supreme Court found that the appellant's arguments were based on a "misreading of the order of the High Court."

It clarified that the High Court did not order a full "new trial" but merely remanded the case to provide the appellant with a procedural safeguard—an opportunity to recall witnesses and adduce evidence in response to the amended charge.
The Court determined that this action was a proper exercise of the High Court's wide powers under the Cr. P. C.

Furthermore, the Court concluded that no prejudice was caused to the appellant. The amended charge was for the same offence (under Section 406), arose from the same "one and indivisible" transaction, and the appellant was explicitly given a full opportunity to meet the new case. Therefore, the amendment was not unfair or prejudicial.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention, holding that the High Court did not err. The High Court's decision to amend the charge and keep the appeal pending while giving the appellant an opportunity to respond to the amendment was a valid exercise of its powers under the Criminal Procedure Code and did not cause any prejudice to the appellant.

issue.issue_text: Whether the amendment of the charge at the appellate stage, when the prosecution had not sought it during the trial, caused prejudice to the accused.

facts: At the appellate stage in the High Court, after the case had been argued for a considerable time, the prosecution made an oral application to amend the charge against the accused.
The original charge was for misappropriation of money under s. 406 of the Penal Code.
The amendment sought to add an alternative charge for misappropriation of goods, which were purchased with the money from the same transaction.
The High Court allowed the amendment and sent the case back to the trial court, directing a 'new trial on this amended charge' to give the appellant a 'full opportunity to meet this case'.
law: The Criminal Procedure Code (Cr. P. C.) gives ample power to both trial and appellate courts to alter or amend a charge.
Section 423 Cr. P. C. invests the appellate court with very wide powers, including the power to make any amendment that may be just or proper.

The primary limitation on this power is that the accused must not be prejudiced. Prejudice occurs if the accused has to face a charge for a completely new offense or is not given a full opportunity to meet the charge and present a defense.

Section 535 Cr. P. C. provides that a finding is not invalid merely because a charge was not framed, unless it has occasioned a failure of justice. If it has, the appellate court can order a charge to be framed and the trial to be recommenced from that point.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the High Court's order did not cause prejudice to the accused.
The amended charge was not for a 'new offence' but was an alternative charge under the same section (406) arising from the same 'one and indivisible' transaction.

Crucially, the High Court's order provided a safeguard against prejudice by sending the case back specifically to give the accused a 'full opportunity' to defend against the amended charge. This included the ability to recall witnesses and adduce fresh evidence.

The Supreme Court interpreted the High Court's direction for a 'new trial' not as a complete retrial from the beginning, but as a procedural step to ensure the accused could respond to the amended charge before the appeal was decided.

The Court reasoned that if the trial court could have framed such an alternative charge initially, the appellate court could also do so, provided it ensured the accused was not prejudiced by the timing of the amendment.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, concluding that no prejudice was caused, or was likely to be caused, to the accused by the amendment of the charge. The High Court acted within its wide powers under the Criminal Procedure Code, and its order included the necessary safeguards to give the accused a full and fair opportunity to meet the amended charge, thereby preventing any prejudice.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was obligated to record its reasons for finding a prima facie case to justify the amendment of the charge.

application.point: The Supreme Court acknowledged that the High Court did not provide specific reasons for finding a prima facie case for the amended charge.
text_evidence: It 1s true that the court did not give any reasons as to why it thinks there was a prima facie case...

application.point: The Court suggested a possible justification for this omission, speculating that the High Court, as an appellate court, wanted to avoid giving an impression that it had already formed a particular view on the evidence, which could prejudice the ongoing proceedings.
text_evidence: ...but being an appellate court perhaps it was anxious to avoid giving an impres-sion that it has taken any particular . view on the evi-dence.

application.point: The Court noted a procedural flaw in the accused's appeal, pointing out that this specific objection was not raised in the Special Leave Petition.
text_evidence: The accused raised no ground on this account in the Special Leave Petition...

application.point: The Supreme Court ultimately decided not to interfere with what it considered a "judicial exercise of discretion" by the High Court, especially since the accused was given a full opportunity to recall witnesses and present fresh evidence, thus preventing any prejudice.
text_evidence: ...nor do we think on this account we should interfere with the judicial exercise of discretion of the learned Judge in framing the charge and in· giving the accused an opportunity to recall any witnesses or adduce fresh evidence on his behalf.

application.point: The Court reasoned that if there was no objection to the trial court framing the original charge, it was difficult to see how an objection could be raised to the appellate court framing an alternative charge based on the same underlying allegations.
text_evidence: If no objection could be taken to the trial Court in framing the original charge it is difficult to see how an objec-tion can be taken at this stage to the framing of ap. alternate charge on the same allegation in the complaint.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the High Court was not obligated to record its reasons for finding a prima facie case. The Court treated the High Court's action as a valid exercise of judicial discretion, noting that the accused had not raised this issue in their petition and, more importantly, was not prejudiced because they were given a full opportunity to defend against the amended charge. The Court also reasoned that the High Court likely avoided giving reasons to prevent influencing the trial's outcome.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred by amending the charge and keeping the appeal pending, instead of first delivering a finding on the charge for which the appellant was convicted.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's challenge to the High Court's order implies the argument that the court should have first decided the appeal on the merits of the original conviction before taking the step of amending the charge and remanding the case.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (complainant) implicitly argued that the procedure was correct by making the application to amend the charge at the appellate stage, contending it was necessary based on the evidence already on record to ensure justice.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the amendment of the charge at the appellate stage, when the prosecution had not sought it during the trial, caused prejudice to the accused.
appellant_arguments: The complainant could have asked the Magistrate to frame an alternate charge during the trial but failed to do so.
Amending the charge at the appellate stage amounts to framing a 'totally new charge in regard to altogether a new subject matter, namely, alleged entrustment of goods'.
Permitting such an amendment would prejudice the accused in his defence.
respondent_arguments: The evidence led at the trial already showed that not only the money but also the goods purchased with it had been entrusted to the appellant.
Based on the materials already on record, it was 'desirable in the interest of justice to allow the amendment' to include an alternative charge regarding the goods.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was obligated to record its reasons for finding a prima facie case to justify the amendment of the charge.
appellant_arguments: The High Court ought to have considered and recorded its reasons as to whether there was a prima facie case against the accused that would justify framing the amended charge.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, supported by the Supreme Court's reasoning, is that the High Court was not obligated to provide detailed reasons, as an appellate court might be 'anxious to avoid giving an impression that it has taken any particular view on the evidence' before the new trial.

cases.principle: To support the principle that an appellate court has wide and extensive powers under the Code of Criminal Procedure (specifically section 423) to alter a charge, and that Indian law is not subject to the same technical limitations as English law, provided the accused is not prejudiced.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under the Criminal Procedure Code, a court, including an appellate court, has the power to alter or amend a charge, provided that the amendment does not introduce a new offense and does not prejudice the accused by denying them a full opportunity to meet the charge and present a defense.
obiter: The history and technicalities of English criminal law, which may have made it more difficult to justify a variation of a charge, do not limit Indian law, which is governed solely by the Penal Code and Criminal Procedure Code.
An appellate court's decision not to provide reasons for finding a prima facie case for an amended charge may be to avoid giving an impression that it has taken a particular view on the evidence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court held that an appellate court has the discretion to amend a charge based on evidence already on record, even if not requested at trial, and remand the case for a limited trial on the amended charge while keeping the appeal pending. This procedure is permissible provided it does not cause prejudice to the accused, whose rights are sufficiently protected by being given a full opportunity to recall witnesses and adduce fresh evidence to meet the amended charge.
legal_tests_applied: Whether the amendment of a charge at the appellate stage causes prejudice to the accused.
Whether the appellate court's decision to amend a charge and remand for a limited trial constitutes a proper exercise of judicial discretion.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's contention that the High Court ordered a full retrial was based on a misreading of the order; the court only directed a limited proceeding on the amended charge while keeping the appeal pending, a procedure it explicitly chose over the appellant's suggestion to first dispose of the appeal.

No prejudice was caused by the amendment because the alternative charge arose from the same 'one and indivisible' transaction, the complainant intended to rely on the same evidence, and the appellant was given a full opportunity 'to recall any witnesses and adduce any evidence on his behalf'.

The High Court was not obligated to record detailed reasons for finding a prima facie case for the amended charge, as an appellate court might be 'anxious to avoid giving an impression that it has taken any particular view on the evidence' before the new proceedings.

The Court reasoned that 'If no objection could be taken to the trial Court in framing the original charge it is difficult to see how an objection can be taken at this stage to the framing of ap. alternate charge on the same allegation in the complaint.'
why_respondent_won: The High Court's procedure was deemed correct, as it specifically rejected the appellant's request to first dispose of the appeal and instead found it 'desirable and proper to keep this pending till the opportunity that is being given to the appellant-accused No. 2 to meet this new case is fully availed of'.

The amendment was justified because the alternative charge for misappropriation of goods was part of the same transaction as the original charge for misappropriation of money, and the complainant stated no new evidence would be led.
The procedural safeguard of allowing the appellant 'to have full opportunity to meet this case' by recalling witnesses or adducing new evidence was sufficient to cure any potential prejudice.
policy_considerations: An appellate court should be cautious not to prejudice the outcome of a remanded trial, and therefore may be 'anxious to avoid giving an impression that it has taken any particular view on the evidence' by not providing detailed reasons for finding a prima facie case to amend a charge.

The core principle of justice requires that an accused be given a full and fair opportunity to defend against any charge, which is satisfied by allowing the accused to recall witnesses and present new evidence after a charge is amended at the appellate stage.
